title: Signature Bound Sufficiency Proofs
description: Signature edition: bounds are never arbitrary — each BMC run records a sufficiency argument (unwinding assertions, diameter arguments, or explicit residual risk) so 'clean up to bound k' is an honest, reviewable claim. The bound's justification is part of the result. This is a Signature original method.
method: Every run files (bound, sufficiency argument, residual risk); reviewers approve the argument, not just the result.
usage: Require sufficiency arguments on all BMC results used for release decisions.

demo.code:
print('result: UNSAT up to k=10')
print('sufficiency: unwinding assertion proved -> bound sufficient, residual risk: none')

title: Signature Loop unrolling strategies
description: Signature edition: The bound is everything in BMC: unroll too little and bugs hide past the bound; unroll too much and the formula explodes. Strategies — unwinding assertions (prove k suffices), incremental deepening, targeted unrolling of suspicious loops — make the bound a deliberate choice, not a guess.
method: Start small, deepen incrementally; add unwinding assertions to prove the bound is sufficient; focus unrolling on loops touching the property.
usage: Document why the chosen bound suffices; use unwinding assertions where the property allows.

demo.code:
print('k=5: UNSAT | k=10: UNSAT + unwinding assertion holds')
print('bound 10 PROVED sufficient for this property')

title: Signature Witness validation and traces
description: Signature edition: A BMC 'bug found' is only useful if the trace replays: witness validation feeds the satisfying assignment back as concrete inputs and runs the actual program to confirm the violation. Validated witnesses become regression tests; unvalidated ones are just solver output.
method: Extract inputs from the model; execute concretely; confirm the violation; convert to a regression test.
usage: Always validate witnesses concretely before filing bugs; keep validated traces as tests.

demo.code:
print('witness: n=11 -> concrete run overflows at line 42: CONFIRMED')
print('trace saved as regression test')

title: Signature Property-driven slicing
description: Signature edition: Most of a program is irrelevant to any one property. Slicing removes code that can't affect the checked property before encoding, shrinking the SAT formula dramatically. The slice is computed by dependency analysis from the property backwards — smaller formula, same verdict.
method: Backward slice from the property over data/control dependencies; encode only the slice; the verdict on the slice equals the verdict on the whole.
usage: Always slice before encoding; verify the slicer is sound for your language subset.

demo.code:
print('program: 12k lines; slice for property P: 340 lines')
print('formula 40x smaller, verdict identical')

title: Signature Bounded checking of smart contracts
description: Signature edition: Smart contracts are ideal BMC targets: small, high-value, and bugs cost real money. Tools bound-check Solidity for reentrancy, integer issues, and access-control violations before deployment — when the code is immutable, the bound must be checked before it ships.
method: Translate contract to a checkable model; bound loops and call depth; check security properties; fix before deployment.
usage: Check every contract before mainnet; bound call depth and loops realistically.

demo.code:
print('contract Vault: reentrancy check, call-depth bound 3')
print('UNSAT -> no reentrancy within bound; deploy approved')

title: Signature Industrial BMC deployment (hardware)
description: Signature edition: BMC's biggest wins are in hardware: Intel, IBM, and ARM use bounded model checking on chip designs, finding bugs in circuits with billions of states. The methodology — properties as assertions, bounded proofs in CI, bug traces to designers — is the template for BMC at industrial scale.
method: Embed assertions in RTL; run BMC in the design CI; triage traces with designers; track bound coverage per block.
usage: Start with critical blocks; grow bound coverage over time; make traces actionable for designers.

demo.code:
print('block FPU-div: 2,048 properties, bound 50, CI 12min')
print('0 violations -> tapeout gate passed')

title: Signature Bit-precise memory modeling
description: Signature edition: BMC's power for C comes from bit-precise modeling: every integer is its actual bitvector, every pointer an address into a modeled heap. Overflows, sign errors, and pointer arithmetic bugs that abstract analyses miss are exactly what bit-blasting catches — the model matches the machine.
method: Model memory as arrays of bitvectors; pointer ops become address arithmetic; the SAT encoding captures wraparound and aliasing precisely.
usage: Rely on bit-precision for arithmetic-heavy code; abstract the heap where full precision explodes.

demo.code:
print('x = INT_MAX; x + 1 -> bitvector wraps to INT_MIN')
print('BMC flags signed overflow precisely (not heuristically)')

title: Signature k-induction for unbounded proofs
description: Signature edition: Bounded checking alone can't prove correctness — but k-induction can: prove the property holds for the first k steps (base case) and that any k consecutive good steps imply the next (inductive step). When both hold, the property holds for all time. BMC finds bugs; k-induction proves their absence.
method: Base: check property for steps 0..k. Step: assume property for k consecutive steps, prove step k+1. Both UNSAT-failures mean proved.
usage: Try k=1 first; increase k when the inductive step fails spuriously; strengthen with auxiliary invariants.

demo.code:
print('k=1: base HOLDS, step HOLDS')
print('property proved for ALL executions (unbounded)')

title: Signature Incremental SAT solving
description: Signature edition: Deepening the bound from k to k+1 shouldn't redo all the work: incremental SAT solvers keep learned clauses across runs, so each deeper check reuses the previous one's reasoning. Incremental BMC turns bound-deepening from quadratic into near-linear cost.
method: Solve under assumptions for bound k; add the k+1 layer as new clauses; re-solve reusing learned clauses; repeat.
usage: Use incremental mode when deepening; keep the solver session alive across bounds.

demo.code:
print('k=10 solved in 3.2s; k=11 reuses clauses -> 0.4s')
print('incremental deepening: 8x faster than fresh solves')
